gist: Fossil fuel carbon emissions are forecast to drop slightly this year.
Higher oil and gas prices from the Iran war drove renewable uptake.
Total carbon emissions still rose due to increased deforestation and land use.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Carbon emissions from fossil fuels are expected to decrease slightly by about 0.4% this year. Oil and gas prices rose due to the war in Iran, prompting people to use less fuel and adopt electric vehicles. However, increased deforestation and land conversion led to higher total global carbon emissions overall.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Scientists warn that this year's reduction might be temporary and insufficient to prevent permanent global heating beyond 1.5C. Remaining carbon budgets are extremely limited, and global emissions must fall rapidly to avoid severe climate impacts.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Analysts note that permanent emission reductions require much greater investments in renewable energy and low-carbon technologies. It remains uncertain whether countries like China will experience sustained emission peaks or if future trends will rebound.

quotes.text: A drop in emissions in one year is not a peak, unless it is driven by structural change.
quotes.role: research professor at the Cicero Centre for International Climate Research

quotes.text: The picture from the Global Carbon Budget is a flatline, not a decline – a projected fall of just 0.4% in 2026, a figure that is unfortunately statistically indistinguishable from zero

sections.text: A 24-year-old gunman drove into Krakow's Main Market Square and opened fire on Saturday. Six people were killed, including a 32-year-old Scottish DJ, four Polish citizens, and an Austrian woman. sections.text: Protesters set up roadblocks and burned passenger vehicles in Bangladesh ahead of protests by supporters of ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina. Prices for fiber-optic material have multiplied due to intense demand and limited supply.
Ukrainian manufacturers are moving spooling in-house to improve quality and lower costs.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Fiber-optic drones have become common in Ukraine and Russia to bypass battlefield electronic jamming. However, importing optical fiber from China has become more costly because drone needs compete with global demand from AI data centers. Russia's massive purchases and tighter ties with China have given it a logistics advantage, while Ukraine faces higher costs, long transport routes, and supply shortages.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The competition for optical fiber strains supply chains and drives up prices significantly. Defective imported spools can cause drones and missions to fail, forcing Ukrainian manufacturers to adapt by bringing the spooling process in-house and performing strict quality control.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Manufacturers continue to navigate long delivery times, border logistics, and security risks. Companies must rely on specialized training, equipment configuration, and flight testing to maintain consistent production quality.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The US Food and Drug Administration ordered manufacturers of GLP-1 weight-loss and diabetes drugs, including Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, Zepbound and Soliqua, to add warning labels about nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. NAION is a rare condition caused by reduced blood flow to the optic nerve, which can lead to sudden and permanent vision loss in one eye.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: An FDA review of clinical trials and studies indicated an increased risk of NAION among GLP-1 users. However, Novo Nordisk and the American Academy of Ophthalmology noted that a direct cause-and-effect link has not been established. Patients taking these drugs often already have separate NAION risk factors, such as diabetes and high blood pressure.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The American Academy of Ophthalmology advises patients not to stop taking GLP-1 medications without speaking to their doctor, and to consult an ophthalmologist immediately if sudden vision loss occurs.

sections.text: Solange Alexandre, one of France's last World War Two resistance heroes, has died aged 104 at a nursing home in Le Mans. British officers attended the French searches while investigating allegations involving Al Fayed.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: French police raided three properties linked to Mohamed Al Fayed, including the Ritz Paris hotel, Villa Windsor in Paris, and a villa in Saint-Tropez. Suspects were taken into police custody for questioning before being released. British Metropolitan Police officers attended the mid-October operations. Several alleged victims were also interviewed. Article 2 calls the Saint-Tropez property Castel Sainte-Thérèse, while French prosecutor statements refer to Villa Sainte-Thérèse.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The searches are part of a preliminary French investigation into allegations of human trafficking by an organised group, aggravated pimping, and rape. Campaign groups praised the French authorities' approach and urged British police to conduct similar searches of Fayed properties.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: French authorities are analysing digital material seized during the searches, and investigations continue under the Paris Public Prosecutor's Office. Survivor groups want the National Crime Agency to take over the investigation in Britain.

gist: Independent Games Festival judges released a statement declining to vote for games using generative AI.
House House disclosed minimal AI use to fix a bug in Big Walk, sparking controversy.
Observers and jurors are divided on whether zero tolerance for minimal AI use is productive.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Nineteen IGF jurors published a statement refusing to vote for games using generative AI in any capacity. Following this, Big Walk developer House House disclosed that it sparingly used LLMs to help fix a difficult Unity engine bug near the end of development, representing well under 0.1 percent of the game's code.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The disclosure ignited a debate within the indie gaming community over transparency and zero tolerance policies. Some jurors argue that any AI use undermines human creativity and labor, while others feel transparency should be weighed against the scale of usage.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Jurors are urging the IGF to adopt a strong anti-clear policy for future years, while developers grapple with how disclosures will affect award consideration and community reception.

timeline.text: Train attack driver's '10 seconds' to change line

gist: A train driver testified about his actions during a stabbing incident on his service.
The driver diverted the train to Huntingdon after hearing reports of an attacker.
Anthony Williams is on trial facing multiple charges of attempted murder.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Andrew Johnson, an LNER train driver, testified at Cambridge Crown Court regarding a stabbing incident. While travelling at high speed, he received an alarm indicating a door was being tampered with. Upon hearing passengers screaming about a knifeman, he decided to divert the train to Huntingdon station. He requested police assistance and performed an unscheduled stop to allow passengers to escape.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The court is examining the actions of the driver during a violent event. sections.text: The Bank of England raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4%. The National Institute of Economic and Social Research criticised this move as too timid, warning it could lead to inflation remaining above the 2% target until 2030. sections.text: Experts argue that failing to take aggressive action risks embedding inflation into the economy as workers seek salary increases. There are concerns that the UK faces a double whammy of high energy prices and rising global borrowing costs, with critics suggesting the government and the Bank are deferring necessary decisions.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The institute forecasts UK economic growth will slow to 0.9% by 2028. Future inflation levels remain dependent on global oil prices and potential shifts in international policy.

sections.text: Louise Casey, head of the social care commission, is set to warn that England's social care system is a chaotic patchwork lacking clear leadership. She argues that standards vary significantly by location and that regulation is often ineffective. Casey intends to call for a new settlement based on shared values of decency and duty.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The current lack of system stewardship makes it difficult to implement improvements or translate policy into practice. This systemic weakness was highlighted by the Covid-19 inquiry, which found that care homes received insufficient protection during the pandemic. Experts warn that structural changes alone cannot fix these issues without genuine political determination.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The Prime Minister has accelerated the Casey review to next year. The government plans to use savings from scrapping the state pension triple lock to fund a new national care service, potentially modelled on the Scottish approach.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A report by the parliamentary and health service ombudsman revealed that disabled people in England wait up to two years for wheelchairs. Complaints regarding NHS wheelchair provision rose significantly. Issues include delays in receiving equipment or parts, and poor repairs. The investigation identified a regulatory gap where services like assessment and fitting are not supervised by health professionals, leaving them outside the remit of the Care Quality Commission.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Delays have profound consequences for users, including physical pain and emotional distress. Many are unable to attend school, access therapy, or maintain independence. The report notes that integrated care boards often lack reliable information on local needs and struggle with an uncompetitive market dominated by a few private firms.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Former Guardian data journalist Mona Chalabi published her first book, Ten Lives, which mixes journalism, data visualisation and memoir. She followed eleven subjects, including herself, across ten income deciles in the US over a five-year period to explore how wealth shapes their lives.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The book argues that collective ignorance and silence around personal income sustain an unfair system. It shows how systemic problems like lack of affordable care can easily overturn lives, driven by a fear of financial futures under advanced capitalism.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Chalabi concludes that society needs a proper societal safety net with a well-funded government spending enough on healthcare, education, and welfare, starting with greater openness about personal wealth.

To challenge our silence around individual income and tackle economic problems causing insecurity.

timeline.text: AI has made it ‘close to impossible’ to assess university coursework, regulator says

gist: AI makes assessing university coursework close to impossible according to a regulator investigation.
The Office for Students warns that degree credibility is under threat from AI use.
Universities are urged to return to traditional exams and in-person presentations.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: An investigation by the Office for Students and Advance HE found that artificial intelligence use in essays, dissertations and open book exams is widespread. Lecturers stated that coursework is now overwhelmingly written with the help of artificial intelligence, threatening academic integrity and making student assessment close to impossible.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The regulator warned that failing to design valid measures of students knowledge and skills could breach registration conditions and lead to sanctions. The situation presents a generational risk to the system, threatening to undermine students learning and institutional assessment abilities.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The Office for Students will continue working with universities and colleges to help them manage risks while reaping benefits. Institutions are encouraged to use more artificial intelligence free assessments, such as in-person written exams, oral examinations, and process-based tasks.

fivew: A regulator reported that artificial intelligence has made assessing university coursework close to impossible.
Widespread unpunished use of artificial intelligence in essays and exams threatens degree credibility.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Hundreds of schools across Scotland, Northern Ireland, the Republic of Ireland and Italy received hoax bomb threat emails on Wednesday. Police assessed the threats as non-credible, noting they originated from generic distribution lists outside the UK. While most schools operated as normal, some local authorities evacuated pupils as a precaution.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The threats caused concern to pupils, parents and staff, coming less than a month after a similar wave of hoaxes. Authorities reassured the public that there was no credible risk, preventing widespread disruption.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Specialist cyber-crime officers and law enforcement bodies in the UK and overseas are working to identify those responsible. Schools have been advised to remain open and stay vigilant.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Consultant doctors in England have paused a two-day strike that was scheduled for 25 and 26 November. The British Medical Association, representing the doctors, decided to suspend the action to engage in formal negotiations with the government regarding pay and working conditions.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The strike would have limited hospital services to emergency care only, likely causing delays for routine and elective procedures. The Health Secretary, Yvette Cooper, stated that the cancellation is positive news for patients and the NHS, allowing staff to focus on winter service delivery.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Formal talks between the British Medical Association and the government are expected to begin soon. Both parties have expressed a desire to discuss pay, working hours, and reforms to improve flexibility and patient care.

sections.text: Google DeepMind has unveiled AlphaGenome 2, an AI model designed to predict how genetic variants affect individual cell types and states. Trained on over 100 million cell profiles, the model provides a more detailed view of gene expression than its predecessor.

sections.text: Understanding how specific genetic changes impact particular cells is crucial for medical research. By identifying these effects, scientists can better target proteins and cell types when developing new treatments for diseases.

timeline.text: BMI alternative for identifying obesity ‘could prevent misdiagnosis in millions’

gist: A new obesity diagnostic approach could reduce misdiagnosis rates globally.
The method combines BMI with waist measurements and organ function tests.
Experts suggest this approach improves individual healthcare and resource allocation.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Medical experts have proposed a new diagnostic approach for obesity to replace the current reliance on BMI. By incorporating waist measurements, weight-to-height ratios, and organ function tests, the method aims to distinguish between healthy individuals and those with harmful excess body fat. Researchers tested this approach using health records from over 800,000 people across four countries.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: BMI is considered a blunt instrument that frequently misclassifies millions of people. The new system identifies clinical obesity, where fat impairs organ function, versus pre-clinical obesity. This allows for more precise medical interventions, ranging from lifestyle advice to surgery, ensuring resources are used more effectively and safely.

fivew: Francisco Rubino and colleagues conducted the research.
A new diagnostic approach for obesity has been proposed to replace BMI.
The study results were published in Nature after testing records spanning 15 years.

The current BMI system leads to widespread misdiagnosis of obesity.

timeline.text: Argentine lawyer mocks UK’s sovereignty claim in Falklands oil case

gist: Argentina challenged UK oil drilling near the Falkland Islands at an international tribunal.
Argentina argues the UK acts like a colonial power regarding disputed maritime resources.
The UK maintains the tribunal lacks jurisdiction over sovereignty and disputes the urgency.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Argentina appeared before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea in Hamburg. Legal representatives argued that the UK should not unilaterally authorise oil drilling in the North Basin of the Falkland Islands. Argentina requested a suspension of the Sea Lion project, citing a long-standing sovereignty dispute. The UK government countered that the tribunal lacks jurisdiction over sovereignty matters and argued that the project should proceed.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The dispute highlights ongoing tensions over the Falkland Islands, which Argentina claims as the Malvinas. Argentina contends that unilateral resource exploitation undermines its rights and represents colonial behaviour. Conversely, the UK maintains that the project is vital for the islands' economy and that the tribunal is not the appropriate venue for resolving the underlying sovereignty disagreement.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The UK is scheduled to provide further submissions to the tribunal. The panel of 20 judges will consider whether to order a suspension of drilling, which is currently planned to commence in March next year.

fivew: Legal teams representing Argentina and the UK.
Argentina is seeking to suspend UK-authorised oil drilling in disputed waters.
The hearing took place in Hamburg during the week of the report.
The case is being heard at the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea.
Argentina claims the drilling violates its rights while the sovereignty dispute remains unresolved.

gist: Linda Noskova defeated Coco Gauff to reach the WTA Finals semi-finals.
Noskova secured victory in straight sets during her tournament debut.
Jessica Pegula eliminated Marta Kostyuk from the competition.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Linda Noskova beat Coco Gauff 6-3 6-3 to become the first player to reach the WTA Finals semi-finals. Noskova served well and hit powerful winners throughout the match. Meanwhile, Jessica Pegula defeated Marta Kostyuk 6-2 7-5 to earn her first win since September.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The victory marks a sixth top-10 win this season for Noskova, who won Wimbledon in July. Gauff struggled on serve, hitting eight aces and eight double faults. Pegula remains in contention for the last four alongside Gauff.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Noskova has secured her place in the semi-finals. Gauff and Pegula can still qualify for the last four.

fivew: Linda Noskova defeated Coco Gauff to reach the WTA Finals semi-finals.
The match took place during the WTA Finals.
The tournament is held in California.
Noskova played with controlled aggression and served brilliantly.

gist: Brighton climbed to second in the Premier League after beating Brentford 2-0.
The Seagulls sit five points behind league leaders Arsenal after ten matches.
Midfielder Pascal Gross downplayed any suggestions that his side are in a title race.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Brighton defeated Brentford 2-0 at the Amex Stadium on Sunday afternoon. The victory lifted the Seagulls into second place in the Premier League, moving them above Manchester City before the November international break.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Brighton have won seven of their opening ten matches, establishing themselves as the closest challengers to league leaders Arsenal with a five-point gap. Their strong underlying numbers and defensive record suggest they could maintain this early-season form.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Brighton head into the international break aiming to maintain their momentum for the remainder of the campaign, while awaiting the return of injured players like Kaoru Mitoma.

articles.standfirst: It was a Premier League classic at Old Trafford but what has Manchester United's 4-4 draw with Aston Villa done to Michael Carrick's future?

timeline.text: Bizarre & thrilling theatre as Carrick's Man Utd future still in limbo

gist: Manchester United drew four-all with Aston Villa after scoring a stoppage-time equaliser.
Manager Michael Carrick remains in his position despite United dropping into the relegation zone.
Fans protested against club owners and ticket prices amid poor league form.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Manchester United drew four-all against Aston Villa in an eight-goal thriller at Old Trafford. United fought back twice from two goals down, securing a point with a ninety-sixth-minute equaliser from Patrick Dorgu. The result left United in eighteenth place in the relegation zone during the international break.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: United are in their lowest league position for forty years after playing at least ten matches, having failed to win a league game since August. The poor form has intensified pressure on manager Michael Carrick and sparked unprecedented fan protests against ticket prices and club ownership.
